title: Interventional Processes For Causal Uncertainty Quantification
claim: The causal settings we study are identified through adjustment criteria, despite unobserved confounding, via back-door or front-door structures.
layout: 2 panels side by side, causal graphs, dashed colored bidirected confounder edges
description: Two causal DAGs side by side on a white background, drawn with circled nodes and black directed arrows. The left graph has four nodes: B and C on top, A and Y on the bottom. C points to B, B points to A, B points to Y, C points to Y, and A points to Y. A dashed blue double-headed arrow links B and A. A dashed red double-headed arrow links C and Y. These show unobserved confounding. The right graph is a simple chain A → M → Y. A long dashed blue double-headed arc links A and Y, showing hidden confounding of the treatment-outcome relationship. Node labels are italic math letters. Colour is used only on the dashed confounder edges. The eye goes first to the colourful dashed arcs against the black structure. The figure is minimal and has no text beyond the node labels.
caption: Left: causal graph where $O = (A,B,C,Y)$ and $(B,C)$ satisfies the back-door criterion w.r.t. $(A,Y)$. Right: Causal graph where $O=(A,M,Y)$ and $M$ satisfies the front-door criterion w.r.t. $(A,Y)$. Definitions of these criteria are in [ref]. Dashed edges = effect of unobserved confounders.
abstract: Reliable uncertainty quantification for causal effects is crucial in high-stakes applications, but remains challenging when the target is an entire function rather than a scalar estimand. In this work, we introduce a GP-based approach for uncertainty quantification of interventional functions. The central idea is to build on recent work representing interventional functions as an inner-product of observational functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS), by constructing appropriate GP priors for such functions and inferring posteriors from observational data. Our approach yields closed-form posterior moments and tractable training and inference, while avoiding pathologies of previous GP prior constructions for RKHS functions. We further derive a practical procedure for posterior coverage calibration. Across synthetic benchmarks, causal Bayesian optimization tasks, and a large-scale real dataset, our method improves uncertainty quantification while remaining competitive in causal effect estimation.
